focus: Early smallness is framed as the lightest and fastest moment a company will have. The goal is to avoid accumulating unnecessary weight.
coreClaim: Keep the organization light so mistakes, priorities, and opportunities can be handled without massive energy.

centralConcept.name: organizational lightness
centralConcept.plainDefinition: Mass is anything that makes a company harder to change: long contracts, excess staff, permanent policies, heavy process, debt, or fixed assumptions. Less mass preserves maneuverability.
centralConcept.whyItMatters: A reader can notice and avoid commitments that make future adaptation expensive.

keyClaims: Every added commitment can increase the force required to change direction. [18.1]
Low mass makes mistakes cheaper to fix and decisions easier to revise. [18.2]
Growth naturally adds weight, so unnecessary weight should be resisted early. [18.3]
Mass includes mental commitments as well as physical assets and payroll. [18.4]
A lean company can change priorities without dragging a large machine behind it. [18.5]

namedExamples.label: smallest fastest earliest-stage company
namedExamples.summary: The essay points out that a new company is often the smallest, leanest, and fastest it will ever be. That moment should be protected rather than hurriedly buried under obligations.
namedExamples.teachesWhat: Flexibility is easiest before the company makes heavy promises.

hardEdge: The misreading is to avoid all commitment. The edge is to distinguish useful structure from weight that reduces future options.

testableFacts.claim: Keeping a company light lets it handle mistakes, priorities, and opportunities without massive energy.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: because low mass means fewer commitments to unwind, so changing direction costs less force.
testableFacts.commonError: a company should lock in as much structure and process as early as possible to look serious.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: heavy early structure adds mass that makes every later change expensive, which is the opposite of the chapter's goal.

testableFacts.claim: Mass is anything that makes a company harder to change, including long leases, large payroll, debt, custom infrastructure, internal process, old code, fixed roadmaps, meetings, and policies.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: because each of these is a commitment that must be migrated, coordinated, or unwound before the company can turn.
testableFacts.commonError: mass is mostly about physical things like office furniture or headcount.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: mass also includes contracts, code, process, and roadmaps, so counting only physical assets understates the weight.

testableFacts.claim: Mass includes mental commitments such as pride in a decision that no longer works, not just physical assets and payroll.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: because an emotional attachment to an old decision resists change as surely as a signed contract does.
testableFacts.commonError: only tangible commitments like staff and assets count as weight a company carries.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: fixed assumptions and pride also raise the force needed to change, so ignoring them undercounts mass.

testableFacts.claim: Every added commitment can increase the force required to change direction.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: because the heavier the company becomes, the more energy it takes to turn.
testableFacts.commonError: adding commitments has no cost as long as each one seems individually reasonable.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: commitments accumulate into mass, and the chapter's point is that this weight compounds the cost of any future change.

testableFacts.claim: Low mass makes mistakes cheaper to fix and decisions easier to revise.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: because a light company can reverse course without dragging a large machine behind it.
testableFacts.commonError: scale and built-up infrastructure make a company better at correcting its mistakes.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: more mass means more to undo, so heavier companies pay more to fix the same mistake, not less.

testableFacts.claim: A new company is often the smallest, leanest, and fastest it will ever be, and that early stage should be used well.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: because early on there are fewer customers to migrate, fewer employees to coordinate, and fewer promises to unwind.
testableFacts.commonError: a startup should rush to take on obligations early so it does not look small.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: burying the early lightness under premature weight wastes the one moment when change is cheapest.

testableFacts.claim: 37signals fits the less-mass idea because it repeatedly favors fewer features, fewer people, and fewer obligations.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: because choosing less in each of these dimensions keeps changing direction possible.
testableFacts.commonError: 37signals stays small mainly to cut costs rather than to preserve agility.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: the chapter frames fewer features, people, and obligations as a way to keep change possible, not primarily as a budget tactic.

testableFacts.claim: Less mass does not mean avoiding all commitment; the skill is telling useful structure from weight that reduces future options.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: because some commitments create trust and capability, so treating lightness as blanket indecision misses the point.
testableFacts.commonError: to stay light a company should refuse to commit to anything.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: refusing all commitment confuses lightness with indecision and forgoes commitments that build trust and capability.

testableFacts.claim: The test for adding mass is whether the same learning can happen with a smaller promise.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: because if a lighter commitment would teach the same thing, the extra weight is added casually and avoidably.
testableFacts.commonError: if a commitment might help eventually, it is always worth taking on now.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: taking on weight that a smaller promise could replace adds mass casually, which the chapter warns against.

voiceCues: treats agility as something to preserve
paraphraseNotes: The Go section closes by naming the hidden cost of commitments. Mass is not only office furniture or staff size. It can be a long lease, a large payroll, custom infrastructure, debt, internal process, old code, fixed roadmaps, meetings, policies, or pride in a decision that no longer works. The heavier the company becomes, the more energy it takes to turn. Early stage work is uniquely light: fewer customers to migrate, fewer employees to coordinate, fewer promises to unwind. The essay asks founders to use that moment well and resist premature weight. 37signals' small-team model fits because the company repeatedly favors fewer features, fewer people, and fewer obligations as a way to keep changing possible. The downstream handoff should avoid treating lightness as indecision. Some commitments create trust and capability. The point is to avoid adding mass casually, especially when the same learning can happen with a smaller promise. Growth naturally adds weight, so unnecessary weight should be resisted early.
